sentences.text: The genus name Cimoliopterus translates to "Cuvier's chalk wing," combining Greek words for chalk and wing.
Estimating the animal's size is difficult due to incomplete fossils, though Bowerbank once estimated a wingspan of about 16.6 feet.
It can be distinguished from related pterosaurs by a premaxillary crest that begins further back on the snout.
Rodrigues and Kellner described the genus in 2013, concluding that A. cuvieri differed enough from relatives to warrant a new monotypic genus.

A single tooth originally reported in the holotype snout had disappeared by the time it was examined in the 2000s. Richard Owen assigned a long bone catalogued as NHMUK PV 41637 to Pterodactylus cuvieri in 1851, identifying it as a possible phalanx bone of the wing-finger. Harry Govier Seeley later placed Pterodactylus cuvieri in the new genus Ptenodactylus in 1869 in an index of specimens at the Woodwardian Museum.
Much of the skeleton was likely pneumatized, filled with air sacs that lightened the body, while forelimbs were proportionally enormous compared to legs, featuring very long wing-fingers.
The animal would have been covered in pycnofibres and had extensive wing-membranes supported by long wing-fingers.
It possibly fed while flying by dipping its long jaws into water to catch fish with interlocking teeth.
In 2019, it was classified within the family Cimoliopteridae and the clade Targaryendraconia, and is closely related to Aetodactylus, a pteranodontoid found in Cenomanian strata in Texas.
Camposipterus is considered the closest relative of Cimoliopterus.
Rodrigues and Kellner considered P. fittoni, O. brachyrhinus, and O. enchorhynchus too fragmentary to assign to Cimoliopterus, classifying them as nomina dubia.
Fossils date to the Cenomanian stage, and the animal lived between 100.5 and 89.8 million years ago during the Cenomanian to Turonian stages in what is now England and the United States.

It is debated whether the premaxillary crests were used to stabilize jaws during feeding or served as display structures. It is uncertain whether C. colorhinus had a crest because all known specimens are incomplete. It is also debated whether Ornithocheirus brachyrhinus and Pterodactylus fittoni belong to Cimoliopterus cuvieri, as they share characteristics but are too incomplete for definitive referral, leading Rodrigues and Kellner to classify them as nomina dubia.
